title: Python: solving the intersection
caption: NumPy gives the same intersection as the two plotted equations.
notes: Every code state is a complete Python example. The residual checks the computed solution against the original system. These small integer examples are well-conditioned. Floating-point equality generally requires a tolerance.
steps:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., -1.], [-1., 2.]])
b = np.array([0., 3.])

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., -1.], [-1., 2.]])
b = np.array([0., 3.])
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(x)  # [1. 2.]

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., -1.], [-1., 2.]])
b = np.array([0., 3.])
x = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
print(x)  # [1. 2.]
print(A @ x - b)  # [0. 0.]
assert np.allclose(A @ x, b)

title: Python: the weights are coordinates
caption: The blue column plus twice the orange column reaches the green target.
notes: Array slicing with A[:,0] selects the first column. The at-sign is matrix multiplication. Compare a weighted sum of columns with the same computation as A @ x. They are identical operations.
steps:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., -1.], [-1., 2.]])
a1, a2 = A[:, 0], A[:, 1]

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., -1.], [-1., 2.]])
a1, a2 = A[:, 0], A[:, 1]
b = a1 + 2 * a2
print(b)  # [0. 3.]

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2., -1.], [-1., 2.]])
a1, a2 = A[:, 0], A[:, 1]
b = a1 + 2 * a2
print(b)  # [0. 3.]
x = np.array([1., 2.])
assert np.allclose(b, A @ x)
print(A @ x)  # [0. 3.]

title: Python: three equivalent products
caption: AB and BA transform the same unit square into different parallelograms.
notes: The code compares the usual product with multiplication by columns and a sum of outer products. The plot compares AB with BA, which is a different operation. Shapes match here because both matrices are square.
steps:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2, -1], [-1, 2]])
B = np.array([[1, 2], [0, 1]])
C = A @ B

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2, -1], [-1, 2]])
B = np.array([[1, 2], [0, 1]])
C = A @ B
by_columns = np.column_stack(
    [A @ B[:, j] for j in range(2)])
assert np.allclose(C, by_columns)

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2, -1], [-1, 2]])
B = np.array([[1, 2], [0, 1]])
C = A @ B
by_columns = np.column_stack(
    [A @ B[:, j] for j in range(2)])
assert np.allclose(C, by_columns)
terms = [np.outer(A[:, k], B[k])
         for k in range(2)]
by_outer = sum(terms)
assert np.allclose(C, by_outer)
print(C)      # [[2, 3], [-1, 0]]
print(B @ A)  # [[0, 3], [-1, 2]]

title: Python: reducing both halves together
caption: The right half becomes A⁻¹. Multiplying by A recovers the identity.
notes: The first two columns hold A and the last two hold I. The same operations act on all four columns. Once the left half is I, slicing the right half gives the inverse. Numerical applications usually solve directly instead of explicitly forming inverses.
steps:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1., 3.], [2., 7.]])
aug = np.column_stack((A, np.eye(2)))

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1., 3.], [2., 7.]])
aug = np.column_stack((A, np.eye(2)))
aug[1] -= 2 * aug[0]
aug[0] -= 3 * aug[1]

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1., 3.], [2., 7.]])
aug = np.column_stack((A, np.eye(2)))
aug[1] -= 2 * aug[0]
aug[0] -= 3 * aug[1]
inverse = aug[:, 2:]
print(inverse)  # [[7, -3], [-2, 1]]
assert np.allclose(aug[:, :2], np.eye(2))
assert np.allclose(A @ inverse, np.eye(2))

title: Python: transpose and row permutation
caption: The entries keep their values as a 2 × 3 array becomes 3 × 2.
notes: A.T is a transpose. The permutation P has the cyclic order used in the next Manim clip. It multiplies R=A.T on the left, producing rows two, three, one. Transposing P reverses that permutation.
steps:
import numpy as np
A = np.arange(1, 7).reshape(2, 3)
print(A.shape)  # (2, 3)

import numpy as np
A = np.arange(1, 7).reshape(2, 3)
print(A.shape)  # (2, 3)
R = A.T
print(R.shape)  # (3, 2)
print(R)  # [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]

import numpy as np
A = np.arange(1, 7).reshape(2, 3)
print(A.shape)  # (2, 3)
R = A.T
print(R.shape)  # (3, 2)
print(R)  # [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]
P = np.array([[0, 1, 0],
              [0, 0, 1],
              [1, 0, 0]])
print(P @ R)  # [[2, 5], [3, 6], [1, 4]]
assert np.allclose(P.T @ P, np.eye(3))

title: Python: closure examples and a counterexample
caption: The blue line contains zero. The shifted orange line misses zero.
notes: Finite examples illustrate closure but do not prove it for every vector. The algebraic equation y=2x proves closure in this case. The negative of q=(1,1) gives a decisive counterexample for the first quadrant.
steps:
import numpy as np
u = np.array([1, 2])
v = np.array([-2, -4])
assert u[1] == 2*u[0]
assert v[1] == 2*v[0]

import numpy as np
u = np.array([1, 2])
v = np.array([-2, -4])
assert u[1] == 2*u[0]
assert v[1] == 2*v[0]
w = 3*u - 2*v
print(w)  # [7 14]
assert w[1] == 2*w[0]

import numpy as np
u = np.array([1, 2])
v = np.array([-2, -4])
assert u[1] == 2*u[0]
assert v[1] == 2*v[0]
w = 3*u - 2*v
print(w)  # [7 14]
assert w[1] == 2*w[0]
q = np.array([1, 1])
assert np.all(q >= 0)
print(np.all(-q >= 0))  # False

title: Python: testing whether b belongs to C(B)
caption: Appending (4, 8) adds no direction. Appending (4, 7) increases the rank.
notes: This connects lecture 6 to the rank language in lecture 9. A right-hand side belongs to the column space if adding it as a column leaves the rank unchanged. NumPy estimates numerical rank using a floating-point tolerance.
steps:
import numpy as np
B = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6]])
r = np.linalg.matrix_rank(B)
print(r)  # 1

import numpy as np
B = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6]])
r = np.linalg.matrix_rank(B)
print(r)  # 1
good = np.column_stack((B, [4, 8]))
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(good) == r)
# True: the target is in C(B)

import numpy as np
B = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6]])
r = np.linalg.matrix_rank(B)
print(r)  # 1
good = np.column_stack((B, [4, 8]))
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(good) == r)
# True: the target is in C(B)
bad = np.column_stack((B, [4, 7]))
assert np.linalg.matrix_rank(good) == r
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(bad) == r)
# False: the target is outside C(B)

title: Python: adding a nullspace vector
caption: The two displayed basis vectors generate the entire nullspace plane.
notes: The columns of N are (-2,1,0) and (-3,0,1). B@N=0 checks both basis vectors at once. For any real parameter pair, xp+N@parameters remains a solution for b=(4,8). The picture shows the homogeneous plane, not the shifted solution plane.
steps:
import numpy as np
B = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6]])
N = np.array([[-2, -3], [1, 0], [0, 1]])
assert np.allclose(B @ N, 0)

import numpy as np
B = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6]])
N = np.array([[-2, -3], [1, 0], [0, 1]])
assert np.allclose(B @ N, 0)
xp = np.array([4., 0., 0.])
x = xp + N @ np.array([0.5, 1.0])
print(x)  # [0.  0.5 1. ]

import numpy as np
B = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6]])
N = np.array([[-2, -3], [1, 0], [0, 1]])
assert np.allclose(B @ N, 0)
xp = np.array([4., 0., 0.])
x = xp + N @ np.array([0.5, 1.0])
print(x)  # [0.  0.5 1. ]
assert np.allclose(B @ x, [4, 8])
print(B @ x)  # [4. 8.]

title: Python: coordinates in a different basis
caption: The same vector (3, 2) has coordinates (1, 2) in the skew basis.
notes: The columns of V are the new basis vectors. Solving Vc=v finds the basis coordinates, while V@c reconstructs the vector in standard coordinates. The vector itself stays fixed. Both bases have dimension two.
steps:
import numpy as np
V = np.array([[1., 1.], [0., 1.]])
v = np.array([3., 2.])

import numpy as np
V = np.array([[1., 1.], [0., 1.]])
v = np.array([3., 2.])
c = np.linalg.solve(V, v)
print(c)  # [1. 2.]

import numpy as np
V = np.array([[1., 1.], [0., 1.]])
v = np.array([3., 2.])
c = np.linalg.solve(V, v)
print(c)  # [1. 2.]
assert np.allclose(V @ c, v)
assert np.linalg.matrix_rank(V) == 2

title: Python: rank plus nullity
caption: The output space C(M) has dimension 2. The input nullspace has dimension 1.
notes: SciPy returns an orthonormal nullspace basis, so its entries can differ from the integer basis by scaling or sign. It still spans the same line. The assertion checks the defining equation M@N=0 with a numerical tolerance.
steps:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import null_space
M = np.array([[1., 0., 1.],
              [2., 1., 3.],
              [0., 1., 1.]])
r = np.linalg.matrix_rank(M)

import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import null_space
M = np.array([[1., 0., 1.],
              [2., 1., 3.],
              [0., 1., 1.]])
r = np.linalg.matrix_rank(M)
N = null_space(M)
print(r, N.shape[1])  # 2 1

import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import null_space
M = np.array([[1., 0., 1.],
              [2., 1., 3.],
              [0., 1., 1.]])
r = np.linalg.matrix_rank(M)
N = null_space(M)
print(r, N.shape[1])  # 2 1
assert np.allclose(M @ N, 0)
assert r + N.shape[1] == M.shape[1]
print(r, N.shape[1], M.shape[1])  # 2 1 3
